extracted_by: hand, T-0309 — the Democrat read, December 1833
note: Vol. I No. 2. The first Democrat after the first: pages 1, 2 and 4 are national and foreign reprint, poetry and miscellany, and the town is on page 3 — the editorial column, the advertising, the prices current and the village ordinances. THE STANDING ADVERTISING OF No. 1 IS NOT RE-CLAIMED. Nineteen of the twenty-odd advertisements in this issue are the same setting T-0308 read at 1833-11-26 and this issue's OCR of them is markedly worse, so re-claiming would bank a poorer witness for the same fact; what is claimed here is what is NEW in the week — five advertisers who were not in No. 1 (Brewster Hogan & Co., David Carver, P. F. Peck, P. Pruyne & Co. and the Chicago English and Classical Academy), the town's own news column, three marriages, the constable canvass, the prices current, and the four village ordinances No. 1's printing did not carry legibly. NO POST-OFFICE LETTER LIST: swept for every form the Democrat uses — 'list of letters', 'letters remaining', 'remaining in the post office', 'uncalled for', a signature ending 'P. M.' — for eight hits, every one of them a line of the paper's OWN agent list on page 1 naming an out-of-county postmaster. The hand count is zero printed lists against zero extracted names. The transcription carries the bare `SOURCE PDF PAGE n` banner, which names the SCAN page (this issue opens at scan page 5 because No. 1 occupies 1-4), so the page numbers in every locator here are the resolver's ordinal reading of that banner.

claims.notes: THE MAIL ROUTE THAT MAKES THE TOWN A JUNCTION. Chicago already has the Detroit mail; what this paragraph reports is a second regular route being concluded to St. Louis, which puts the town on a through line rather than at the end of one. It is the earliest statement in this corpus of the reason the place grew, and it is dated three weeks after the paper's first number. THE NAME IS READ AND NOT PRINTED: the transcription gives 'Dr. J. T. Truez', which is not a name anything else in this corpus carries, and the same issue advertises 'JOHN T. TEMPLE' wanting twenty-five to thirty young horses for cash (claim c012) — the purchase a man who has just taken a mail contract makes. Dr. John T. Temple held the Chicago-to-Ottawa/St. Louis mail contract, so the reading is Temple; it is an inference off the horses advertisement and the trip to Washington, recorded here rather than smuggled into the quote, which keeps 'Truez' exactly as the page gives it.

The Indian Agent's OFFICE is a working building of the town in December 1833 — it holds specie, private papers and a trunk of Indian jewelry, and it is close enough to open ground that the thief carried the trunk 'some rods from the Office' and left it there. The agent is Thomas J. V. Owen, who signs the town ordinances of the same month as President of the Board of Trustees (1833-12-24 claims c005-c010); the paper writes 'Office of Col[onel] ... Indian Agent' and the rank is lost at the line edge, so the man is not named in the quote and is not supplied here. The paragraph also records that the town has enough night crime for the editor to warn about 'midnight visiters ... prowling about our town' — the same week the trustees are appointing a collector and an attorney.

entities.role: the townsman at whose house the trustees meet

claims.notes: WHERE THE CORPORATION MEETS, AND IT IS SOMEBODY'S HOUSE. Chicago has been an incorporated town for four months and its Board of Trustees has no room of its own: it meets at Mr. Graves'. The ordinances adopted the day after this notice — 4 December 1833 — are headed 'held at the house of Dexter Graves' when the paper prints them a week later (1833-12-10 c009), which is what identifies the Graves here and dates this meeting to 4 December. Graves' Tavern is also the landmark Matthias Mason & Co.'s blacksmith shop is advertised opposite (1833-12-17 c001), so the same building is the town's public room, its inn and its street reference.

claims.normalized: We are also requested to say, that the old [m]embers of the Chicago Polemical Society, [as] well as such gentlemen as may wish to become [m]embers thereof, will meet at the house next [do]or below J. Wright's store, on Thursday even[in]g the 5th instant.
claims.notes: A DEBATING SOCIETY, MEETING IN A HOUSE IDENTIFIED BY THE SHOP NEXT TO IT. The Chicago Polemical Society already has 'old members' in December 1833, so it predates the newspaper. What earns the claim is the address: 'the house next door below J. Wright's store'. The town has no street numbers, so a private house is located by the storefront beside it and by which way is DOWN the street — the same grammar every relative placement in this corpus uses. John Wright's store is documented at 1833-11-26 (T-0308 c009, c023) and again in January 1834; nothing in this corpus says which street it stood on, so the house cannot be put on the ground, only beside a shop that also cannot.

Mark Noble jun. marries Charlotte Wesencraft and George Bickerdyke marries Mary Noble 'at the same time, and by the same' — one ceremony, the Nobles marrying out and in. 'Between Clark and Dearborn-streets' is a real address in a town where the cross streets are the landmarks and the long streets are assumed — but it leaves the frontage open, and Clark and Dearborn are one block apart on South Water, Lake, Water and Randolph alike. The stone ware list is the finest-grained inventory in the December papers and is worth keeping whole: covered jars, pots, jugs, pitchers, churns and stone milk pans, sized in quarts and gallons — the pottery of an 1833 kitchen, sold beside window glass and iron.

claims.notes: TWENTY-FIVE TO THIRTY HORSES, FOR CASH, IN ONE ADVERTISEMENT. That is not a townsman buying a saddle horse; it is a stage or mail contractor stocking a line, and it stands in the same issue whose news column reports a regular mail route about to be concluded from Chicago to St. Louis on the news brought back from Washington by 'Dr. J. T. Truez' (c001). The two together are what identifies that man as Dr. John T. Temple. As a claim about the town it says something plainer: somewhere in or near Chicago in December 1833 there is stabling being got ready for thirty horses.

Fifteen hundred bushels standing in one barn 25 miles west on the Dupage, advertised in the Chicago paper, is the supply side of a village that grows none of its own grain — and the distance is stated, which most country advertisements do not do. Sweet is the same man who appraises Harry Boardman's estray mare on the Dupage in this issue's estray notice and in No. 1 (T-0308 c031). claims.notes: A SCHOOL BUILDING ON A NAMED CORNER, FIVE WEEKS AFTER THE SCHOOL WAS FIRST REPORTED. T-0308 c003 has the Democrat's news item that 'a school has recently been established in this village, by Mr. Sproat of Boston'; this is the same school advertising itself with a prospectus, a four-department fee table and — the thing that matters for the ground — an address at the corner of Water and Franklin streets. It is one of only three corner placements this December set carries. The advertisement runs to seventy lines of terms and book lists; the cited range is the heading, the address, the opening sentence and the preceptor's signature, and the lines between them are the fee table, which carries no further claim about the building.

It is also the ordinance that says most about what the town was like: a place where enough people discharged guns in the streets that a two-dollar fine was worth writing down, in the same month as the hog ordinance and the stove-pipe ordinance.

claims.normalized: 7. Be it further Ordai[ne]d, That any person or [persons who] shall after the tenth [d]ay of Decem[ber next, ride or drive any] horse, mare, gelding, mule or [ass at a gallop or immoderate rate] through any of the streets of said town, [shall be liable to] a fine of two dollars for each and every offence, to be collected as above specified.
claims.notes: THE STREETS ARE BUSY ENOUGH TO NEED A SPEED LIMIT. Section 7 is a claim about the town's streets as a surface people use, not as lines on the plat: horses were being ridden through them fast enough, often enough, for the trustees to fine it at the same rate as discharging a firearm. Read beside section 9 — nothing to be thrown into the river — and section 5 — no plank to be taken off either bridge — it is a picture of a town whose public works are a handful of streets, two bridges and a river, all of them being abused. The clause is badly broken and the words 'gallop' and 'immoderate' are read from the sense and bracketed, not supplied silently.

claims.notes: THE STALLION ORDINANCE, AND IT COSTS MORE THAN A GUN. Five dollars against two for firing a weapon in the street. The section is here because it completes the December 1833 ordinance set rather than for the ground it describes — but it does describe ground: stallions were being shown publicly in a town small enough that the trustees legislated the practice by name. Sections 10 and after run off the foot of the column in this printing and are not claimed.
